title: Modern Post-Training: A Deep Dive  — Will Brown, Prime Intellect
talk_summary: Will Brown describes Prime Intellect's open-source post-training stack (Verifiers V1, PrimeRL), decomposing agent evaluation/training into composable task sets, harnesses, and runtimes with an interception-server pattern so real agent harnesses can be evaluated or RL-trained unchanged.

takeaways.technique: Task set / harness / runtime decomposition for evals
takeaways.what_they_do: They separate the data+rules (task set) from the agent loop (harness) from where it executes (runtime), so the same task set can be run against different harnesses or models and swapped freely.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the key pieces we broke things down into were a task set, a harness, and a runtime. And so these are all composable.

takeaways.what_they_do: They keep group-level rewards first-class so you can do pairwise judging, ranking, or bonus the shortest correct answer across multiple samples rather than scoring each rollout independently.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's a lot of things where you really want to do pairwise judging or you want to do ranking

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of a fixed length penalty (unknown optimal length), they compare samples within a group and reward the most concise correct one, incentivizing efficiency without guessing a target.
takeaways.evidence_quote: give a bonus to the ones that are the most concise

takeaways.technique: Interception server / fake base URL for harnesses
takeaways.what_they_do: They give each harness rollout a fake OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible base URL and intercept requests, so any real harness (Codex, Claude Code) runs unchanged and can be pointed at eval, training, or production endpoints.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we are responsible for giving each harness rollout a fake base URL, which could be OpenAI compatible or Anthropic compatible

takeaways.technique: Async rollouts tolerant of long-tail latency
takeaways.what_they_do: They run rollouts asynchronously so forward progress isn't tied to the slowest rollout, accepting mild off-policyness (avg ~16) and letting slow sandbox boot/grading overlap without wasting GPU time.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can go reasonably far off policy. Like I think 16 is where we typically are often operating

takeaways.what_they_do: They maintain both logical message streams and token streams, using a renderers library to avoid re-tokenization/chat-template mismatches that cause subtle bugs in long runs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to be able to maintain these dual streams of the logical text and the the tokens
